claims.text: Targeted Ti and carbon additions during elemental powder processing and spark plasma sintering can promote in-situ TiC formation in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The resulting TiC will occur as uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates within grain interiors and along grain boundaries.
TiC nanoprecipitates act as sinks for irradiation-induced helium and vacancies.
Capture of helium and vacancies by TiC reduces the nucleation and growth of helium bubbles.
Fine TiC precipitates provide dispersion strengthening.
A tungsten-based refractory HEA containing in-situ TiC can retain useful mechanical integrity.
The TiC-containing alloy will have enhanced radiation tolerance relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without deliberately promoted TiC.
Elemental powder mixing is a practical manufacturing route for tungsten-based refractory HEAs.
The proposed benefit will hold under helium-ion irradiation at approximately 900–1000 °C and reactor-relevant fluences.
After irradiation, the TiC-containing alloy will exhibit significantly smaller helium bubbles than the baseline.
After irradiation, the TiC-containing alloy will exhibit a significantly lower helium-bubble density than the baseline.
After irradiation, the TiC-containing alloy will retain or improve hardness relative to the baseline.
After irradiation, the TiC-containing alloy will retain or improve strength relative to the baseline.
The beneficial TiC volume fraction has an optimal range corresponding to roughly a few weight percent, with about 1–8.5% offered as a precedent.
Excessive or inhomogeneously distributed TiC may cause embrittlement or processing difficulties.
Elemental powder mixing followed by spark plasma sintering has produced a tungsten-based HEA containing in-situ TiC.
